english: Your parcel's here / A delivery came
usage: 존댓말 — courier or family member announcing a delivery to you
반말 — to a friend, roommate, or younger family member
격식 — an app/SMS notification or a building intercom announcement
There's a delivery — can you come get it?
Courier at the door checking if you can receive it now
examples: A: 택배 왔어요. / B: 네, 잠깐만요.
A: Your parcel's here. / B: Yes, one moment.
The bare doorstep announcement and the natural response; 잠깐만요 buys a few seconds to get to the door
어, 택배 왔나 봐. 누가 좀 받아 줘.
Oh, looks like a delivery came. Someone grab it.
왔나 봐 = 'looks like it came' — guessing from the doorbell sound, not direct sight
택배 왔는데 지금 집에 아무도 없어서요. 경비실에 맡겨 주시겠어요?
A parcel came but nobody's home right now. Could you leave it at the security office?
Real situation: redirecting a courier when you can't open the door; 경비실 = building security booth
nuance: 택배 왔어요 is the everyday phrase for 'a package arrived', said by a 택배 기사님 (courier) at your door, by a family member who heard the bell, or by an app push notification. Literally it means 'the taxi-delivery came' — 택배 (宅配) refers both to the parcel and the courier service that brings it door-to-door. Register follows the relationship: 존댓말 왔어요 to anyone you don't know well, including the courier; 반말 왔어 inside the family or to a close friend. Automated building notices use the fuller 도착했습니다. The nearest alternative is 배송 왔어요, but 배송 is the abstract shipping-process word stores use (배송 시작, 배송 완료) — it's not natural for the physical box at your door. Critically, do not confuse 택배 with 배달: 배달 is hot-food delivery (치킨, 피자), a completely different service and verb set. The English-speaker trap is trying to name the person — 'the delivery guy is here' — as 배달원이 있어요, which sounds robotic; Koreans simply announce the object: 택배 왔어요.

structuredNuance.t: Literally '택배 came' — 택배 (宅配, door-to-door delivery) is both the parcel and the service. The phrase announces 'a courier package has arrived', used by the courier at your door, a family member who heard the bell, or an app push notification.

존댓말 왔어요 to the courier or any adult you don't know well; 반말 왔어 inside the family or to a close friend; automated notices and official SMS use 도착했습니다. Never say it to a boss to mean 'your parcel arrived' without 주문하신 택배 왔습니다 — a bare 택배 왔어요 to a superior can sound too casual.
배송 왔어요 sounds unnatural for a box at the door — 배송 is a shop's process word (배송 시작/완료). 배달 왔어요 is specifically hot-food delivery (치킨, 피자); using 배달 for a courier parcel is a major category error.
택배 왔어 (반말) → 택배 왔어요 (존댓말) → 택배 도착했습니다 (격식). To redirect: 문 앞에 놔 주세요 / 경비실에 맡겨 주세요.

English speakers try to name the person — '배달원이 있어요' ('the delivery person is here') — which sounds robotic. Also, calling any delivery 배달 왔어요 is wrong if it's a parcel: 배달 = food, 택배 = courier parcel.

mistakes: Saying 배달 왔어요 for a parcel — 배달 is food delivery (치킨, 피자); a courier box is 택배, so the bell-ring announcement is 택배 왔어요.
Calling the courier 택배맨 or 배달원 to their face — the polite term is 택배 기사님 (driver-sir); 기사님 shows respect.
Using 배송 for the box itself (배송 왔어요 sounds off) — 배송 is the shipping process; the arrived parcel is 택배.

english: Please leave it at the door
usage: Please leave it at the door.
존댓말 — to a courier; standard contactless-delivery request
Just leave it by the door.
반말 — to a friend or family member dropping something off
You can just leave it at the door, thank you.
격식/정중 — fuller, very polite written or spoken request
You can just leave it at the door and go.
Natural extension telling the courier they needn't wait
examples: A: 문 앞에 놔 주세요. / B: 네, 알겠습니다.
A: Please leave it at the door. / B: Sure, got it.
The core contactless request and the courier's standard reply; most delivery apps have a 요청사항 box where you type exactly this
지금 손이 안 비어서요. 그냥 문 앞에 놔 주세요.
My hands are full right now — just leave it at the door, please.
그냥 = 'just', softens it and signals the courier doesn't need to wait for you to answer
벨 누르지 마시고 문 앞에 놔 주세요. 아기가 자고 있어서요.
Please don't ring the bell, just leave it at the door — the baby's sleeping.
Real note typed in a delivery-app 배송 요청사항 box; adding the reason makes the request feel natural, not demanding
nuance: This is the contactless-delivery line you say to a courier or type into a delivery app's 요청사항 (request) field. 놔 주세요 is the contracted spoken form of 놓아 주세요 ('please place/put it') — 놔 in speech, 놓아 in careful writing; both are correct. To a stranger-courier use 존댓말 (놔 주세요); to family or a friend 놔 줘. Adding 그냥 ('just') before it softens the request and implies no need to hand it over personally. The near-synonym 두고 가세요 ('leave it and go') adds the nuance that they needn't wait; 놔 주세요 focuses purely on the spot. The classic English-speaker slip is translating 'at the front door' as 앞문에 — 앞문 means the actual door panel (literally 'front door'), whereas 문 앞 means 'the space in front of the door', the location you want. Word order matters: 문 앞 ≠ 앞문.

structuredNuance.t: 놔 주세요 = contracted form of 놓아 주세요, 'please place it (for me)'. 문 앞 = 'in front of the door' (location). The phrase means: put the parcel in the space just outside my door, no need to hand it to me.
Exists in three tiers: 놔 줘 (반말 to family/friends) → 놔 주세요 (존댓말, standard to couriers) → 놓아 주시면 됩니다 (격식, formal written). Typed into the app's 배송 요청사항 box, 존댓말 is expected even though it's text.

두고 가세요 adds the cue 'and you can leave' — the courier needn't wait. 놔 주세요 focuses only on placement. For building-wide contactless, 경비실에 맡겨 주세요 (leave it at the security booth) is the alternative when you're away.
놔 줘 → 놔 주세요 → 놓아 주시면 됩니다. Extensions: 벨 누르지 마시고 문 앞에 놔 주세요 (don't ring), 그냥 문 앞에 두고 가셔도 돼요 (feel free to leave).
앞문에 놔 주세요 ≠ 'leave it at the front door' — 앞문 is the door panel itself; the location 'in front of the door' is 문 앞에. Also: 나 주세요 is unrelated (the verb 나다); it must be spelled 놔 주세요 (from 놓다).

mistakes: Saying 앞문에 놔 주세요 — 앞문 = the front door panel itself; the spot 'in front of the door' is 문 앞에. Particle/word-order matters.
Using 놓으세요 as a bare command — to a service person, soften with 주세요 (놔 주세요) so it's a request, not an order.
Writing 나 주세요 for 놔 주세요 — it's 놓다 → 놔, with ㅎ; spelling it 나 changes the verb entirely.

usage: 존댓말 — complaint to a neighbor, staff, or stranger
반말 — to a friend, family, or roommate
격식 — written complaint to 관리실 or a formal report
It's that the upstairs unit is so loud…
Trailing -서요 softens it into a polite lead-in to a request
examples: A: 너무 시끄러워요. / B: 죄송합니다, 조심할게요.
A: It's too loud. / B: Sorry, we'll be more careful.
The bare complaint and the apology you hope to hear back; 조심할게요 = 'I'll be careful' is the standard contrite reply
밤늦게 음악 소리가 너무 시끄러워요. 좀 줄여 주시겠어요?
The music is way too loud late at night. Could you turn it down a bit?
Pairs the description (시끄러워요) with a request (줄여 주시겠어요) — the natural two-step structure for a noise complaint
안녕하세요, 아래층인데요. 밤마다 너무 시끄러워서 잠을 못 자겠어요.
Hi, I'm from the unit below — it's so loud every night I can't sleep.
Real doorstep opener: 아래층인데요 identifies you first, which softens the complaint significantly before the real grievance
nuance: 시끄러워요 is an adjective-based complaint meaning 'it is (too) loud/noisy' — you're describing a state, not accusing someone. 너무 ('too/extremely') intensifies it. Use this to flag noise to a neighbor at the door, to café staff, or in a building complaint. With a stranger keep 존댓말 (시끄러워요); to a friend 시끄러워; a written or formal report upgrades to the noun phrase 소음이 심합니다 ('the noise is severe'). The key difference from 조용히 해 주세요 is direction: 시끄러워요 states the problem, 조용히 해 주세요 requests the fix — Koreans typically lead with the problem and follow with the request. Never open a neighbor complaint with a bare 시끄러워요! without first saying 안녕하세요, 아래층인데요 ('Hi, I'm from downstairs') — unannounced bluntness sounds like a fight, not a polite heads-up. The English-speaker grammar trap: 시끄럽다 is a descriptive verb (adjective), so you never attach it to 해요 — 시끄러워 해요 is not Korean.

structuredNuance.t: 너무 시끄러워요 = 'too noisy (state)'. This describes the current noise level — it is an adjective sentence, not a request. The real function is to open a complaint conversation, usually followed by a request (줄여 주세요, 조용히 해 주세요).

존댓말 시끄러워요 for any adult stranger, neighbor, or public-space staff. 반말 시끄러워 to family or a close friend. Formal written complaints to 관리실 or the landlord prefer 소음이 심합니다 or 소음이 너무 심해서 생활에 불편을 초래하고 있습니다. Never deliver this without introducing yourself first — 안녕하세요, 아래층인데요 is essential social scaffolding.

조용히 해 주세요 = asks for quiet (a request). 너무 시끄러워요 = describes the noise (a statement). Koreans pair them: 너무 시끄러워요, 조용히 좀 해 주세요. 소음이 심하다 is the noun-based formal variant used in reports and 민원 (civil complaints).
시끄러워 (반말) → 시끄러워요 → 소음이 심합니다 (격식). Softened: 조금 시끄러운 것 같아서요 ('it seems a bit noisy, so…'). Strengthened: 정말 너무 시끄러워서 못 견디겠어요 ('it's so loud I can't stand it').

시끄럽다 is a descriptive verb/adjective — you NEVER say 시끄러워 해요 ('do noisy') as if it were an action verb. Also, Korean requires social scaffolding before the complaint; leading with 시끄러워요! alone sounds aggressive to neighbors.

mistakes: Treating 시끄럽다 as an action verb (시끄러워 해요) — it's a descriptive adjective; just say 시끄러워요.
Confusing 시끄럽다 (noisy) with 조용하다 (quiet) — to ask for silence you flip to 조용히 해 주세요, not 시끄럽게 하지 마요 only.
Opening a neighbor complaint with a bare 시끄러워요! — without 안녕하세요/아래층인데요 it sounds like a fight; identify yourself first.

english: Please keep it down a little
usage: 존댓말 — to a neighbor or stranger; 좀 softens the request
반말 — to a friend, sibling, or roommate
격식/정중 — extra-polite -주시겠어요? as a yes/no question, the gentlest form
It's late, so please keep it down.
Adding 밤이라 ('since it's night') gives the request a natural reason
examples: A: 조용히 좀 해 주세요. / B: 아, 죄송해요.
A: Please keep it down. / B: Oh, sorry.
The minimal request and the typical contrite reply; note 죄송해요 rather than 괜찮아요 — the other person acknowledges the fault
여기 도서관이에요. 조용히 좀 해 주세요.
This is a library. Please keep it down.
Stating the place first (도서관이에요) makes the request feel objective and reasonable rather than personal
죄송한데, 애들이 자고 있어서요. 조용히 좀 해 주시면 감사하겠습니다.
Sorry, but my kids are sleeping — I'd really appreciate it if you could keep it down.
Real polite neighbor ask: 죄송한데 opens softly, the reason follows, -면 감사하겠습니다 is the most deferential close
nuance: This is the request form of a noise complaint — you're asking for the fix, not just describing the problem. 조용히 is the adverb 'quietly' (from 조용하다, 'to be quiet'), 해 주세요 = 'please do (it) for me', and 좀 is the key softener: it lowers the illocutionary force from a command to a polite request. Dropping 좀 makes 조용히 해 주세요 noticeably sharper; without both 좀 and 주세요 (just 조용히 해) it sounds like you're scolding a child. Register ladder: 조용히 좀 해 (반말) → 조용히 좀 해 주세요 (존댓말) → 조용히 해 주시겠어요? (가장 정중, question form). Versus 너무 시끄러워요 (describes the noise), this phrase requests the behavior change; Koreans typically lead with the description and follow with the request: 너무 시끄러워요. 조용히 좀 해 주세요. The English-speaker trap is the grammar: 조용히 해 주세요 literally is 'please do (it) quietly', using the adverb 조용히 + 하다; the adjective form 조용해 주세요 (treating 조용하다 as an action) is a learner mistake — the correct structure needs the adverb.

structuredNuance.t: 조용히 좀 해 주세요 = '(please) do (it) quietly, a little, for me'. It is a polite behavioral request — asking someone to act quietly — rather than a statement about noise level. The 좀 is non-optional for politeness.

반말 조용히 좀 해 (to friends, family). 존댓말 조용히 좀 해 주세요 (to neighbors, strangers). 격식 조용히 해 주시겠어요? (softest — question form, best for strangers you don't want to confront). In a written complaint, use 소음을 줄여 주시기 바랍니다.

너무 시끄러워요 describes the problem; 조용히 좀 해 주세요 requests the fix. They are often used in sequence. 조용히 해 주세요 (without 좀) is sharper. 소음 좀 줄여 주세요 ('please reduce the noise') focuses on the level rather than the behavior.
조용히 좀 해 → 조용히 좀 해 주세요 → 조용히 해 주시겠어요? Also: 소리 좀 낮춰 주세요 (turn the sound down), 음악 좀 줄여 주세요 (turn the music down).

The bare imperative 조용히 해 to a stranger (no 좀, no 주세요) sounds like scolding a child in Korean, even though 'please be quiet' in English is perfectly fine. Always use 좀 … 해 주세요. Also: 조용해 주세요 is a learner error — the structure requires the ADVERB 조용히 + 하다, not the adjective form.

mistakes: Dropping 좀 and 주세요 (just 조용히 해) with strangers — it becomes a curt order; the polite form needs 좀 … 해 주세요.
Saying 조용해 주세요 — 조용하다 is an adjective; the request uses the adverb 조용히 + 해 주세요, i.e. 'do (it) quietly'.
Over-literal 'please be silent' as 침묵해 주세요 — 침묵 is heavy/literary ('silence, reticence'); everyday Korean is 조용히 해 주세요.

usage: 존댓말 — reporting to a landlord, staff, or 관리실
반말 — to a friend, family, or roommate
격식 — formal report, message, or written notice
Adding -ㄴ 것 같아요 ('it seems') hedges when you're not 100% sure of the fault
examples: A: 고장 났어요. / B: 언제부터요?
A: It's broken. / B: Since when?
The bare report and the natural diagnostic follow-up; '언제부터요?' asks when it started to assess severity
세탁기가 갑자기 고장 났어요. 어떻게 해야 돼요?
The washing machine suddenly broke. What should I do?
갑자기 ('suddenly') is the most common lead-in for unexpected breakdowns; 어떻게 해야 돼요? signals you want guidance, not just sympathy
관리실이죠? 저희 집 인터폰이 고장 나서 전화드렸어요.
Is this the management office? I'm calling because our intercom is broken.
Real call structure: confirm who you reached (관리실이죠?), then give your name and reason; -나서 connects 'it broke' to 'that's why I'm calling'
nuance: 고장 나다 is the standard phrase for a mechanical or electronic device that has stopped working — elevators, boilers, washing machines, intercoms, phones. It is intransitive: the subject-marked thing 고장 나다 ('breaks, by itself'). To a landlord or office use 존댓말 (났어요); among family 났어; a written report uses 고장이 났습니다. Adding -ㄴ 것 같아요 hedges it when you're unsure: 고장 난 것 같아요. The key dividing line: 고장 나다 is specifically for mechanisms, while 망가지다 ('get wrecked/ruined') is broader — physical objects like toys, zippers, or even a relationship can 망가지다, but only things with a mechanism 고장 나다. A shattering glass is 깨졌어요, not 고장 났어요. The causative 고장 냈어요 ('I caused it to break') exists and matters — using it accidentally blames yourself when you just want to report a fault. English speakers often reach for 부러졌어요 ('snapped in two') for appliances, but that verb is for rigid things that snap — bones, sticks — never an unresponsive TV.

structuredNuance.t: 고장 나다 = literally 'malfunction (故障) occur'. The real meaning: a mechanical/electronic device has stopped functioning. It is intransitive — the device fails on its own. The causative 고장 내다 ('cause to break') is a different and self-incriminating form.

존댓말 고장 났어요 to the landlord, 관리실, repair center, or any adult. 반말 고장 났어 to family or friends. Formal written reports use 고장이 났습니다. When uncertain whether it's a real fault or a settings issue, hedge with 고장 난 것 같아요.

고장 나다 = mechanism fails (appliances, vehicles, electronics). 망가지다 = get ruined/wrecked (broader — any object, including non-mechanical). 깨지다 = shatter (glass, screen). 부러지다 = snap/break in two (sticks, bones, rigid objects). A silent TV is 고장 났어요, not 부러졌어요 or 깨졌어요.
고장 났어 (반말) → 고장 났어요 → 고장이 났습니다 (격식). Hedged: 고장 난 것 같아요. Uncertain: 작동이 안 되는 것 같아요 ('seems not to be operating'). Causative: 고장 냈어요 = 'I broke it (my fault)'.

Mapping 'broken' as 부러졌어요 for an appliance — 부러지다 is for things that snap in two (bones, sticks). A non-functioning device is 고장 났어요. Also: accidentally saying 고장 냈어요 (causative) when you just want to report a fault — that says 'I broke it (my fault)'.

mistakes: Using 부러졌어요 ('snapped') for an appliance — that's for sticks/bones; a non-working machine is 고장 났어요.
Saying 깨졌어요 for a machine — 깨지다 = shatter (glass, screen); a malfunctioning device is 고장 났어요.
Mixing up 고장 났어요 (it broke, by itself) with 고장 냈어요 (I broke it) — the second blames you; use 났어요 to just report the fault.

usage: 존댓말 — to a landlord, repair technician, or 관리실
반말 — to a friend or family member; 고치다 is the everyday casual verb
I'd like to request a repair, please.
격식 — very polite; 부탁드립니다 for a formal written or spoken request
Around when could it be repaired?
Natural follow-up asking for a repair timeline after making the request
examples: A: 수리 좀 해 주세요. / B: 네, 기사님 보내 드릴게요.
A: Please get it fixed. / B: Sure, I'll send a technician.
The repair request and the office's standard response; 기사님 = the technician (literally 'driver-sir', the honorific for any skilled worker)
보일러가 고장 났는데 수리 좀 해 주세요.
The boiler's broken — could you have it fixed?
Pairs naturally after 고장 났어요; the two-sentence structure (state problem → request fix) is the standard complaint pattern
지난번에 말씀드린 곳인데요, 아직 수리가 안 돼서요. 빨리 좀 해 주시면 감사하겠습니다.
It's the place I mentioned last time — it still isn't fixed, so I'd really appreciate it if you could hurry.
Real follow-up chasing an overdue repair; 지난번에 말씀드린 ('as I mentioned last time') references the prior contact, 감사하겠습니다 keeps it polite
nuance: 수리 좀 해 주세요 is the formal-ish repair request you'd make to a landlord, service center, or building office — not to a friend. 수리 (修理) is the Sino-Korean noun for 'repair', paired with 하다; 좀 softens it to a request, 주세요 marks it as polite. The casual everyday equivalent is the pure-Korean verb 고치다: 고쳐 줘 (반말) or 고쳐 주세요 (존댓말). The register split tracks the word choice: 수리 to officials, 고치다 to friends — saying 수리해 줘 to a friend sounds stiff and oddly formal. The dividing line between the two words: 수리 implies a professional paid fix of something mechanical (appliance, vehicle, pipe), while 고치다 is broader and also covers 'correct / mend' (고쳐야 할 버릇 = a habit to fix). English speakers sometimes try 만들어 주세요 ('make it') — 만들다 is 'create from scratch', completely wrong for a repair. Adding 빨리 ('quickly') in a follow-up is natural but should still be wrapped in 주시면 감사하겠습니다 to stay polite.

structuredNuance.t: 수리(를) 해 주세요 = 'please do the repair for me'. 수리 (修理) is the Sino-Korean repair noun. The real function is a formal request directed at a professional or authority (landlord, office, service center), not an equal.

수리 좀 해 주세요 (존댓말, to officials/staff). 수리 좀 부탁드립니다 (격식, most formal). 고쳐 줘 (반말 to friends/family). Never say 수리해 줘 to a friend — it sounds jarringly formal in casual speech. At a service center counter, 수리 맡기고 싶어요 ('I'd like to leave it for repair') is also natural.

수리하다 = professional/paid repair of a mechanism. 고치다 = fix broadly (also: correct a habit, mend clothes). In speech 고치다 is more common; 수리 is more formal/official. Both take 주세요 for the polite request form.
고쳐 줘 (반말) → 고쳐 주세요 / 수리 좀 해 주세요 (존댓말) → 수리 좀 부탁드립니다 (격식). Follow-ups: 언제쯤 수리가 가능할까요? / 빨리 좀 해 주시면 감사하겠습니다.
Trying 만들어 주세요 to mean 'fix it' — 만들다 = create from scratch, not repair. Also: saying 수리해 줘 to a friend sounds stiff; friends say 고쳐 줘. And dropping 주세요 (just 수리해) turns a request into an order.

mistakes: Using 만들어 주세요 to mean 'fix it' — 만들다 = make/create; repairing is 수리해 주세요 or 고쳐 주세요.
Saying 수리해 줘 to a friend — 수리 sounds officialese in 반말; friends say 고쳐 줘.
Dropping 주세요 (just 수리해) when asking staff — it becomes an order; soften to 수리 좀 해 주세요 / 부탁드려요.

usage: 존댓말 — a neighbor or staff member directing you to 관리실
반말 — to a friend, family member, or roommate
You can inquire with the management office.
격식 — formal phrasing; 문의하다 = make an official inquiry
For that, you can just tell the management office.
Natural shorthand for routing a problem to the right place
examples: A: 엘리베이터가 안 돼요. / B: 관리실에 전화해 보세요.
A: The elevator's not working. / B: Try calling the management office.
The classic problem-and-redirect exchange; -해 보세요 = 'try doing', making it a gentle suggestion not a command
주차 문제는 저도 잘 몰라서요. 관리실에 한번 전화해 보세요.
I'm not sure about the parking issue myself — try giving the management office a call.
한번 ('give it a try / once') further softens the suggestion; 저도 잘 몰라서요 first admits the neighbor's own ignorance, which is polite
택배가 자꾸 없어지면 관리실에 전화해서 CCTV 확인해 달라고 해 보세요.
If your parcels keep disappearing, try calling the office and asking them to check the CCTV.
Real advice chaining two actions: 전화해서 ('call and then') … 달라고 해 보세요 ('try asking them to'); practical and natural structure
nuance: In Korean apartment buildings and officetels, the 관리실 (管理室, management office) is the nerve center for all building issues — broken elevators, water outages, heating failures, parking disputes, parcel storage — so this sentence is extremely common when a neighbor or staff member routes you to the right contact. 관리실에 takes 에 ('to a place'); -해 보세요 = 'try doing', which frames it as a gentle suggestion. Register follows the relationship: 존댓말 (보세요) to a neighbor or adult; 봐 in 반말 to a friend. The critical pair to keep straight is 관리실 (maintenance/admin office, handles repairs and billing) vs 경비실 (guard/security booth at the entrance, handles access and parcel receiving). Reporting a broken boiler goes to 관리실; a suspicious stranger at the gate goes to 경비실. English speakers often say 사무실 ('office') but 사무실 is a generic business office; a residential building's maintenance desk is always 관리실. The particle distinction also matters: 관리실에 (toward/at the office) vs 관리실에서 (action taking place at the office) — you call TO the office, so 에 is correct.

structuredNuance.t: 관리실에 전화해 보세요 = 'try (보세요) phoning (전화해) to the management office (관리실에)'. The real meaning: 'the management office is the right contact for this — go there'. It is advice/redirection, not a command.

존댓말 전화해 보세요 when giving advice to a neighbor, visitor, or adult. 반말 전화해 봐 to a friend. Formal written: 관리실로 문의하시기 바랍니다. The -해 보세요 ('try doing') construction is key — dropping 보세요 and saying just 전화하세요 sounds more like an instruction than a tip.

관리실 = maintenance/admin office (repairs, billing, resident registration). 경비실 = security/guard booth (entry control, parcel receiving). They are in different physical locations in the building. A broken boiler → 관리실. Suspicious visitor → 경비실. Parcel left → 경비실.
전화해 봐 (반말) → 전화해 보세요 → 관리실로 문의하시면 됩니다 (격식). Also: 관리실에 말해 보세요 ('try telling the office'), 관리실에 연락해 보세요 ('try contacting the office').

Calling it 사무실 (generic business office) — in a residential building the maintenance desk is 관리실 specifically. Also: 관리실에서 전화해 보세요 is wrong (에서 = action takes place there); you call TO the office, so the destination particle 에 is needed: 관리실에 전화해 보세요.

mistakes: Calling it 사무실 — that's a generic office; an apartment's maintenance desk is 관리실.
Confusing 관리실 (maintenance/admin) with 경비실 (security gate) — boiler/water issues go to 관리실; parcels and entry to 경비실.
Using 에서 instead of 에 (관리실에서 전화해 보세요) — 에서 marks where an action happens; 'call TO the office' takes 관리실에.

english: There's no water / The water won't come out
usage: 존댓말 — reporting to 관리실, landlord, or building staff
반말 — to a roommate or family member
격식 — formal/notice wording; 단수(斷水) = water supply cut
갑자기 frames it as an unexpected outage, signaling urgency
examples: A: 물이 안 나와요. / B: 잠시만요, 확인해 볼게요.
A: There's no water. / B: One moment, I'll check.
The bare outage report and the office's standard response; 확인해 볼게요 = 'I'll go and check'
아침부터 화장실 물이 안 나와요. 혹시 단수예요?
There's been no water in the bathroom since morning — is the supply cut off, maybe?
혹시 단수예요? checks whether it's a planned outage (단수 = supply cut); if yes, it's building-wide and you just have to wait
온수가 안 나와서 찬물로 씻었어요. 보일러 문제일까요?
No hot water came out so I washed with cold — could it be the boiler?
Real situation: distinguishing 온수 (hot water, boiler issue) from a full 단수 (supply cut) — they need different fixes and different contacts
nuance: This reports a water failure — no flow from taps — to your building office or landlord. 나오다 ('come out') is the verb Koreans use for water, gas, and electricity flowing from a source; 안 negates it. The phrase is 물이 안 나와요, not 물이 없어요 (which means 'there is no water in stock', like a depleted water bottle). Learn the crucial sub-variants: if only hot water is out, say 온수가 안 나와요 — this points to a boiler issue, not a supply cut; if cold water also fails, it's likely a 단수 (斷水, water cut-off), which is building-wide. Register: to officials 존댓말 (나와요); to family 나와; official outage notices say 단수(가) 됐습니다 or 단수 예정입니다. The English-speaker trap is 물이 안 돼요 — 되다 ('work/function') applies to machines, not water flow; water flows out with 나오다. Another is 물이 없어요 for a dead tap, which implies no water supply anywhere, not a blocked flow.

structuredNuance.t: 물이 안 나와요 = 'water isn't coming out'. The verb 나오다 ('come out') is the natural Korean frame for fluid flow from a tap or pipe — not 있다/없다 (existence) and not 되다 (function). The phrase reports the physical absence of flow.

존댓말 안 나와요 to 관리실, landlord, or building staff. 반말 안 나와 to family. Formal notices use 단수(가) 됐습니다 or 금일 단수 예정입니다. If contacting the office by text, writing 현재 저희 세대 물이 안 나오고 있습니다 sounds appropriately formal.

온수가 안 나와요 = only hot water is out (→ likely a boiler fault). 물이 안 나와요 = no water at all (→ likely a supply cut, 단수). 단수 = official planned or emergency water supply cut, building-wide. The fix and the contact differ, so specifying the right phrase matters.
물이 안 나와 (반말) → 물이 안 나와요 → 단수가 됐습니다 (격식). Variants: 온수가 안 나와요 (hot water only), 수압이 약해요 (water pressure is low), 혹시 단수예요? (checking if it's an outage).

물이 안 돼요 is wrong for a dead tap — 되다 = work/function (for machines); water flow uses 나오다. 물이 없어요 means 'there is no water (in supply/stock)' — correct for a depleted bottle, wrong for a closed tap. Use 물이 안 나와요.

mistakes: Saying 물이 안 돼요 — 되다 is for devices; water flowing from a tap uses 나오다, so 물이 안 나와요.
Using 물이 없어요 for a dead tap — 없다 = 'there's none (in supply/stock)'; a non-flowing faucet is 안 나와요.
Saying just 물이 안 나와요 when only hot water is out — specify 온수가 안 나와요 so they check the boiler, not the mains.

usage: 존댓말 — reporting to landlord or 관리실
반말 — to family or a roommate
격식 — formal report; 작동(作動) = operation/functioning
I turned the boiler on but it's not working.
틀었는데 ('I turned it on but…') shows you already tried the normal way
examples: A: 보일러가 안 돼요. / B: 에러 표시 떠 있어요?
A: The boiler isn't working. / B: Is there an error code showing?
The bare report and the practical diagnostic follow-up — checking for an error display is the first step the office always asks about
날도 추운데 보일러가 안 돼서 집이 너무 추워요.
It's cold out and the boiler's not working, so the place is freezing.
The natural complaint linking the season to the urgency; 너무 추워요 escalates the urgency beyond a mere inconvenience
보일러를 아무리 틀어도 온수가 안 나와요. 사람 좀 보내 주실 수 있어요?
No matter how I run the boiler, no hot water comes out — could you send someone?
Real call: 아무리 …아도 ('no matter how') conveys repeated failed attempts; 사람 좀 보내 주실 수 있어요? = 'can you send a technician?'
nuance: The 보일러 (gas boiler for 온돌 floor heating and hot water) is the most critical appliance in a Korean home, making 보일러가 안 돼요 a high-urgency winter complaint. 안 되다 = 'doesn't work/function', the standard phrase for a device that won't operate; subject takes 가/이. This overlaps with 고장 났어요, and the dividing line matters: 안 돼요 describes 'it's not working right now' — potentially a setting or reset issue — while 고장 났어요 asserts 'it's definitively broken'. If you're unsure, 안 돼요 is the safer, softer opening report; the technician will determine if it's truly 고장. Note also the 온돌 connection: Korean floor heating means the whole home is cold when the boiler fails, which is why even mild boiler trouble is treated urgently. The English-speaker trap is spelling/confusion: 돼요 is the correct contracted form of 되어요 (되 + 어요 → 돼요); 되요 is a widespread but incorrect spelling. A second trap: 보일러가 안 해요 uses 하다 ('do'), wrong for a device's function — use 되다.

structuredNuance.t: 보일러가 안 돼요 = 'the boiler doesn't work/function'. 되다 is the verb for a device or system functioning; 안 되다 negates it. The real meaning: something is preventing the boiler from operating, and the speaker doesn't yet know if it's a setting or a real fault.

존댓말 안 돼요 to the landlord, 관리실, or building staff. 반말 안 돼 to family. Formal: 보일러가 작동이 안 됩니다. In winter, this is an urgent matter — mention 춥다 (cold) when reporting so the office treats it as a priority.

안 돼요 = 'not working now' (could be a reset issue, may not be truly broken). 고장 났어요 = 'it's broken/faulty' (asserts a fault). If you're unsure, open with 안 돼요; if it's confirmed broken after checking, escalate to 고장 났어요. 작동이 안 됩니다 is a formal synonym.
보일러가 안 돼 (반말) → 보일러가 안 돼요 → 보일러가 작동이 안 됩니다 (격식). Extensions: 보일러를 틀었는데 안 돼요, 온수가 안 나와요, 에러 뜨고 있어요 (error code showing).
Writing 보일러가 안 되요 — the contraction of 되어요 is 돼요, not 되요; 되요 is an extremely common misspelling but incorrect. Also: 보일러가 안 해요 is wrong — 하다 is for doing an action; a device's functioning uses 되다.

mistakes: Writing 보일러가 안 되요 — the contraction of 되어요 is 돼요; 되요 is a common misspelling.
Saying 보일러가 안 해요 — 하다 is for doing an action; a device that won't function uses 되다, so 안 돼요.
Calling any boiler issue 고장 났어요 immediately — if it might be a setting/reset, the safer report is 보일러가 안 돼요.

english: How do I do the recycling separation?
usage: How do I separate the recycling?
존댓말 — asking a neighbor or 관리실
How do you do the recycling?
반말 — asking a friend or roommate
How should the recycling be sorted?
격식 — formal/polite; -하면 됩니까 sounds official or written
Which bin does this go in?
Practical extension asking where a specific item goes
examples: A: 분리수거 어떻게 해요? / B: 요일 정해져 있어요. 수요일이에요.
A: How do I do the recycling? / B: There's a set day — it's Wednesday.
The bare question and a typical first answer; collection days vary by building and neighborhood
이사 와서 잘 몰라서요. 분리수거 어떻게 해요?
I just moved in and don't really know — how do I sort the recycling?
이사 와서 ('since I moved in') gives the reason for not knowing; it signals you're a newcomer and invites a full explanation
플라스틱이랑 비닐은 따로 버려야 돼요? 분리수거 처음이라 잘 몰라서요.
Do plastic and plastic film go separately? It's my first time sorting and I'm not sure.
Real question getting at the hardest distinction: 플라스틱 (rigid plastic) vs 비닐 (soft film/bags) — these go in different bins
nuance: 분리수거 (分離收去, separate collection) is the mandatory household recycling-sort system in Korea — every apartment has dedicated bins for 플라스틱, 캔, 유리, 종이, 비닐, and sometimes 스티로폼, with fixed collection days that vary by building and district. Newcomers genuinely need to ask, and this question is perfectly natural to put to a neighbor or the 관리실. 분리수거(를) 어떻게 해요? = 'how do I do the sorting?'; the items are 버리다 ('thrown out / put out'). The critical related category is 음식물 쓰레기 (food waste), which has a completely separate bin and is NOT part of 분리수거 — mentally they are different streams. The English-speaker trap is asking 재활용 어떻게 해요? — 재활용 (recycling as an abstract concept) is technically correct but sounds like asking a policy question; the household act of sorting-and-putting-out is called 분리수거. Also: 비닐 (soft bags/film) and 플라스틱 (rigid plastic containers) go in separate bins — treating them as one 'plastic' pile is the most common newcomer sorting mistake.

structuredNuance.t: 분리수거 = 分離收去, 'separate removal' — the household act of sorting waste into categories before building collection. The question 어떻게 해요? asks 'how do I physically carry this out?', not an abstract policy question.
존댓말 어떻게 해요? to any neighbor or 관리실 staff. 반말 어떻게 해? to a friend. Asking a neighbor is completely normal and welcomed — Koreans expect newcomers to ask. The 관리실 will often hand you a printed schedule.

재활용 어떻게 해요? sounds like a policy question; 분리수거 어떻게 해요? is the natural household-chore phrasing. 음식물 쓰레기 is a separate stream entirely — different bin, different bag (often a paid 음식물 종량제 봉투), different day.
어떻게 해? (반말) → 어떻게 해요? → 어떻게 하면 됩니까? (격식). Specifics: 플라스틱은 어떻게 버려요?, 비닐은 따로 버려야 돼요?, 분리수거 날이 언제예요?

Asking 재활용 어떻게 해요? — 재활용 is the abstract recycling concept; the household sorting act is 분리수거. Also: treating 비닐 (soft bags/film) and 플라스틱 (rigid containers) as one category — they go in separate bins in most Korean buildings.

mistakes: Asking 재활용 어떻게 해요? — 재활용 is the concept 'recycling'; the household sorting act is 분리수거.
Putting 음식물 쓰레기 in with 분리수거 — food waste is a separate collection; keep it out of the recycling bins.
Confusing 비닐 (soft film/bags) with 플라스틱 (rigid) — they're separate categories; lumping them gets your bag rejected.

usage: 존댓말 — classifying an item for someone else
반말 — to a roommate or family member
Food waste must be disposed of separately.
격식 — building notice; 배출하다 = put out/discharge (official term for waste disposal)
Can you take out the food waste?
Everyday chore request to a housemate; 버리다 = throw out / dispose of
examples: A: 이거 음식물이에요? / B: 아니요, 그건 일반 쓰레기예요.
A: Is this food waste? / B: No, that's general trash.
The core sorting question and the key contrast — 일반 쓰레기 (general trash) is what food waste is NOT; knowing both terms is essential
음식물 쓰레기는 물기 빼고 버려야 돼요.
You have to drain the liquid before throwing out food waste.
물기 빼고 ('drain the moisture first') is a standard rule in most Korean buildings; excess liquid causes odor and may result in a rejected bag
달걀 껍데기랑 뼈는 음식물 아니에요. 일반 쓰레기로 버리세요.
Eggshells and bones aren't food waste — put them in general trash.
Real edge case that catches everyone: hard shells and bones look like food but are classified as 일반 쓰레기 because animals can't eat or decompose them easily
nuance: 음식물 쓰레기 (飮食物 쓰레기, 'food-stuff garbage') is the mandatory compostable waste stream in Korean homes, separate from both 일반 쓰레기 (general trash) and 분리수거 (recyclables). It goes into a dedicated bin or a paid 음식물 종량제 봉투 (volume-rated bag), and there are strict rules about what counts. The key test is: 'can an animal eat it / will it readily decompose?' — so cooked vegetables, fruit peels, and leftover rice are 음식물; but 달걀 껍데기 (eggshells), 뼈 (bones, including fish bones), 조개껍데기 (shellfish shells), 씨앗 (large seeds), and 양파 겉껍질 (onion outer skins) all go to 일반 쓰레기. Register: 이에요/예요 to classify something; 버리다 for the act; formal notices use 배출하다. The English-speaker trap is assuming 'anything from the kitchen = food waste'; the Korean definition is narrower, based on animal-edibility. Also: saying 음식 쓰레기 is wrong — the fixed compound form requires 음식물 (음식물, with 물).

structuredNuance.t: 음식물(飮食物) = 'food and drink stuff' (the broad category of consumables). 쓰레기 = garbage/waste. The real meaning is the specific compostable food-waste stream in Korea's mandatory separation system — not simply 'kitchen trash'.
Everyday: 이거 음식물이야/이에요? (asking to classify) / 음식물 쓰레기 버려 줘/주세요 (chore request). Formal notices: 음식물 쓰레기는 별도 배출하시기 바랍니다. With a landlord explaining rules: 음식물은 따로 버려야 해요 (이에요).

일반 쓰레기 = general waste bag (includes eggshells, bones, shells, non-recyclable packaging). 분리수거 = sorted recyclables (plastics, cans, paper, glass). 음식물 쓰레기 = only the compostable, animal-edible food scraps. The three streams are mandatory and separate.
음식물 쓰레기 (full form) → 음식물 (shortened in context: 이거 음식물이야?). Actions: 버리다 (casual 'throw out'), 배출하다 (formal 'discharge/put out'). Bags: 음식물 종량제 봉투 (the specific paid bag required in many areas).

Thinking 'food waste = anything from the kitchen' — in Korea the test is 'could an animal eat it / will it compost easily', so eggshells, bones, and shells go to 일반 쓰레기 not 음식물. Also: saying 음식 쓰레기 (without 물) — the correct fixed compound is 음식물 쓰레기.

mistakes: Putting eggshells/bones in 음식물 쓰레기 — only soft, rot-able food qualifies; shells and bones go to 일반 쓰레기.
Saying 음식 쓰레기 — the fixed term is 음식물 쓰레기 (음식물, not 음식).
Throwing it out wet — most areas require 물기 빼고 (drained); excess liquid can get it rejected or fined.

usage: The noise from upstairs is hard to deal with.
존댓말 — describing the problem to a neighbor or office
The inter-floor noise is really bad.
반말 — venting to a friend or family member
I filed a complaint regarding inter-floor noise.
격식 — formal; 민원(民願) = civil complaint, 넣다 = file/submit
윗집 층간 소음 때문에 잠을 못 자요.
I can't sleep because of the noise from the unit above.
Naming 윗집 ('upstairs unit') pinpoints the source
examples: A: 층간 소음이 심해요. / B: 관리실에 말해 보셨어요?
A: The inter-floor noise is really bad. / B: Have you told the management office?
The bare complaint and the standard practical response — going through 관리실 (not confronting directly) is the expected Korean approach
윗집 발소리랑 의자 끄는 소리, 층간 소음이 너무 심해요.
Footsteps and chair-dragging from upstairs — the inter-floor noise is just too much.
Lists the two classic culprits: 발소리 (footsteps) and 의자 끄는 소리 (chair-dragging sound) — knowing these words helps you explain the specific issue to 관리실
층간 소음 때문에 직접 올라가지 말고 관리실 통해서 얘기하는 게 좋아요.
For inter-floor noise, it's better to go through the management office rather than confronting them directly.
Real advice embedded in Korean apartment culture: 직접 올라가다 ('go up yourself') is risky — escalation is common; using 관리실 as a buffer is the culturally expected and safer route
nuance: 층간 소음 (層間騷音, 'between-floors noise') is the most emotionally loaded term in Korean apartment life. It covers footsteps, running children, dragged furniture, late-night music, and any vibration that travels from one unit's floor to the ceiling of the unit below. It's a set compound phrase — you use it as a unit, never build it on the spot. The adjective partner is 심하다 ('severe'): 층간 소음이 심해요. You report it via 관리실 (management office) or file a 민원 (civil complaint). A crucial cultural note: direct confrontation between neighbors over 층간 소음 is notorious in Korea for escalating dangerously — residents are strongly advised to go through intermediaries (관리실, 층간소음이웃사이센터). The English-speaker trap is inventing 바닥 소리 ('floor sound') or 아래층 소리 ('downstairs sound') — Koreans don't use these; the recognized fixed term is 층간 소음 and no one will misunderstand it. Plain 소음 alone lacks the specific apartment-conflict connotation.

structuredNuance.t: 층(層) = floor/story, 간(間) = between, 소음(騷音) = noise. Literally 'between-floors noise'. The real meaning is the specific social problem of noise traveling through the floor/ceiling structure of an apartment building — the term carries significant cultural and legal weight in Korea.

존댓말: 층간 소음 때문에 힘들어요 / 층간 소음이 심해요 (to neighbors, 관리실). 반말: 층간 소음 진짜 심해 (venting to friends). Formal: 층간 소음 민원을 접수하고 싶습니다 (to the office or legal body). Culturally: always go through the 관리실 first, not directly to the neighbor.

소음 = noise (generic). 층간 소음 = specifically the between-unit apartment noise conflict, with all its cultural and legal implications. 생활 소음 = lifestyle noise (broader — can include street noise or music). When discussing an upstairs neighbor complaint, use 층간 소음 specifically.
층간 소음이 심해요 (it's severe) / 때문에 힘들어요 (it's hard because of it) / 민원을 넣다 (file a complaint). Culprits: 발소리 (footsteps), 의자 끄는 소리 (chair dragging), 아이들 뛰는 소리 (kids running).

Inventing 바닥 소리 ('floor sound') or 아래층 소리 — Koreans use the fixed term 층간 소음. Also: attempting to confront the neighbor directly (as English-speakers typically might) — in Korean apartment culture, going directly is seen as risky and aggressive; 관리실을 통해서 (through the office) is the expected path.

mistakes: Saying 바닥 소리 or floor 소음 — the recognized term is the fixed compound 층간 소음.
Using plain 소음 when you mean the upstairs/downstairs conflict — specify 층간 소음 so people know the situation.
Confronting the neighbor with a bare complaint — culturally you route it 관리실을 통해서 (through the office) to avoid escalation.

usage: 존댓말 — reporting to 관리실 or warning neighbors
반말 — to a friend or family member
The elevator is broken and under inspection.
격식 — wording on a posted notice; 점검 중 = under maintenance/inspection
Variant for when it halts mid-run or gets stuck, not fully out of service
examples: A: 엘리베이터가 고장 났어요. / B: 계단으로 가셔야겠네요.
A: The elevator's broken. / B: Looks like you'll have to take the stairs.
The bare report and the practical consequence; 계단으로 가셔야겠네요 = 'it seems you'll have to go by stairs' — softened with 겠네요
엘리베이터가 또 고장 났어요. 이번 주만 벌써 두 번째예요.
The elevator's broken again — that's already the second time this week.
또 ('again') signals a recurring problem; this framing is a common real complaint to 관리실 requesting better maintenance
안에 사람이 갇혔어요! 엘리베이터가 고장 났어요. 빨리 관리실에 연락해 주세요!
Someone's trapped inside! The elevator's broken — please call the office quickly!
Emergency framing: 갇혔어요 ('is trapped') comes first because it changes the urgency; the cause (고장) is secondary in an emergency call
nuance: This is the real-situation report you make to the 관리실 or warn fellow residents about when the lift is out — important in tall Korean apartment buildings where many residents are elderly or carry heavy loads. 엘리베이터 (loanword from English/French; formal/older term is 승강기 升降機) takes 가/이 as subject, and the breakdown verb is 고장 나다. The distinction between 고장 났어요 (broken, out of service) and 멈췄어요 / 갇혔어요 (stopped mid-run / someone is trapped) is practical: the second is an emergency requiring an immediate call, not just a maintenance ticket. English-speaker traps: calling it 리프트 (리프트 in Korean = ski lift or hydraulic jack, not a building elevator), or translating 'the elevator is down' literally as 엘리베이터가 내려갔어요 — that simply means 'the elevator went down a floor'. Also: in casual sign-language shorthand, Koreans write just 엘리베이터 고장 (no particle) on a notice — but in spoken sentences the subject particle 가 is needed.

structuredNuance.t: 엘리베이터가 고장 났어요 = 'the elevator has had a malfunction occur'. 고장 나다 is intransitive. The real meaning: the elevator is out of service, not merely 'went down' — it requires a maintenance call, not just waiting.

존댓말 고장 났어요 when reporting to 관리실, posting a warning note, or telling a neighbor. 반말 고장 났어 to family. Posted notices use 고장 나서 점검 중입니다 / 운행 중지 ('service suspended'). If someone is trapped, drop register — just shout 갇혔어요! 관리실!

고장 났어요 = out of service (report, not emergency). 멈췄어요 = it stopped mid-floor (may or may not be an emergency). 갇혔어요 = someone is trapped inside (emergency). 운행 중지 = 'service suspended' (official notice language). Know which applies — they trigger very different responses.
고장 났어 (반말) → 고장 났어요 → 고장 나서 점검 중입니다 (격식). Upgrade variants: 엘리베이터가 멈췄어요 (stopped), 갇혔어요 (trapped — emergency). 승강기 is the formal/technical synonym for 엘리베이터.

Saying 리프트 for the elevator — in Korean, 리프트 = ski lift or hydraulic jack. The word is 엘리베이터. Also: 엘리베이터가 내려갔어요 = 'the elevator went downstairs' (normal movement), not 'is down/broken'. 'Out of order' = 고장 났어요 / 운행 중지.

mistakes: Saying 엘리베이터가 내려갔어요 to mean 'out of order' — that means it descended a floor; broken is 고장 났어요.
Calling it 리프트 — in Korean 리프트 is a ski lift/jack; the building lift is 엘리베이터 (or 승강기).
Confusing 고장 났어요 (broken/out of service) with 멈췄어요/갇혔어요 (stopped/trapped) — the latter is an emergency; call 관리실 at once.

usage: 존댓말 — asking a host, landlord, or staff
반말 — asking a friend or family member
May I ask what the passcode is?
격식/정중 — softer, more refined way to ask; 어떻게 되나요? is politely indirect
Could you tell me the Wi-Fi password?
Common extension specifying which password you need
examples: A: 비밀번호가 뭐예요? / B: 공일이삼사예요.
A: What's the passcode? / B: It's 01234.
The bare question and how the number is actually said: 공 = 0, not 제로; 공일이삼사 is how Koreans read aloud digit strings like door codes
현관 비밀번호가 뭐예요? 손에 짐이 많아서요.
What's the front-door code? My hands are full.
현관 ('entrance/front door') specifies the door lock; 짐이 많아서요 gives the reason naturally without being demanding
체크인했는데요, 도어록 비밀번호가 안내된 거랑 달라서요. 다시 좀 알려 주시겠어요?
I've checked in, but the door-lock code is different from what was provided — could you tell me again?
Real Airbnb/officetel situation: 도어록 = the keypad lock unit; 안내된 거랑 달라서요 = 'it's different from what was given to me' — polite but clear
nuance: Korean homes and residential buildings overwhelmingly use keypad door locks (도어록 or 번호키), so 비밀번호가 뭐예요? is an essential phrase for any tenant, guest, or Airbnb visitor. 비밀번호 (秘密番號, 'secret number') covers door codes, Wi-Fi passwords, and PIN numbers broadly; 뭐예요? is the direct polite ask, while 어떻게 되나요? is softer and more roundabout (implying 'what might it be?'). To a host or landlord it's 존댓말; to a friend 비밀번호 뭐야. The casual shortening is 비번 (비밀번호 → 비번), common in texting and speech between friends. The near-synonym 암호 ('cipher/code') exists but feels technical or cinematic; everyday passwords and PINs are 비밀번호. English speakers often reach for 패스워드 — understood but foreign-sounding; 비밀번호 is native and universal. A practical digit trap: Koreans read 0 as 공 in digit strings (not 제로), and announce * as 별표 and # as 샵 or 우물 정자 on keypads, so listen for these when someone reads you a code.

structuredNuance.t: 비밀번호(秘密番號) = 'secret number'. 뭐예요? = 'what is it?'. The real use covers door keypad codes, Wi-Fi passwords, ATM PINs — any secret numeric or alphanumeric code. In Korean homes the most common application is the front door keypad, making this phrase essential for any visitor.
존댓말 비밀번호가 뭐예요? to a host, landlord, or staff. 반말 비밀번호 뭐야? to friends or family. Most polite: 비밀번호가 어떻게 되나요? (어떻게 되나요? is an indirect, deferential question form). Casual shortening: 비번이 뭐야? / 비번 알려 줘.

암호 = cipher/code (feels spy-like or technical; not for everyday door codes). 패스워드 = loanword from English (understood, but foreign-sounding). 비번 = casual shortening of 비밀번호, common in speech and chat. 도어록/번호키 = the physical keypad device itself.
비밀번호 뭐야? (반말) → 비밀번호가 뭐예요? → 비밀번호가 어떻게 되나요? (가장 정중). Extensions: 와이파이 비밀번호, 공동현관 비밀번호, 현관 비밀번호. Change requests: 비밀번호 바꿔도 될까요?

Defaulting to 패스워드 — understood but not native; say 비밀번호. Also: reading 0 as 제로 — in Korean digit strings it is 공 (공일이삼 = 0123). Asking 비밀번호가 어디예요? is wrong — 어디 = where; the value is 뭐 (what): 비밀번호가 뭐예요?

mistakes: Defaulting to 패스워드 — it's understood but the natural word is 비밀번호 (casual 비번).
Reading 0 as 제로 in a code — Koreans say 공 (공일이삼 = 0123); using 제로 sounds off for door/phone codes.
Asking 비밀번호가 어디예요? — 어디 = 'where'; to ask the value use 뭐예요? or 어떻게 되나요?.

usage: 존댓말 — inviting a guest, neighbor, or visitor inside
Come on in for a bit.
반말 — to a close friend or younger person
Would you like to come in for a moment?
격식/정중 — question form is the most deferential; gives the visitor the option to decline
일단 ('first of all') warmly ushers them in before any discussion
examples: A: 잠깐 들어오세요. / B: 아니에요, 여기서 받을게요.
A: Come in for a moment. / B: Oh no, I'll take it here.
The warm doorstep invite and a polite decline — 여기서 받을게요 = 'I'll receive it right here', the natural way to stay outside
밖에서 얘기하기 그러니까 잠깐 들어오세요.
It's awkward to talk out here, so come in for a bit.
얘기하기 그러니까 ('since it's awkward to talk out here') is the indirect Korean reason — implying inconvenience rather than demanding
어머, 비 많이 오는데 잠깐 들어오세요. 차 한잔 드시고 가세요.
Oh my, it's pouring — come in for a moment. Have a cup of tea before you go.
Real neighborly warmth: the weather reason + 드시고 가세요 ('have some and go') is a complete hospitable package, showing the cultural value of 정 (warm connection)
nuance: This is the warm invitation a host gives at the door — to a neighbor returning something, a courier bringing good news, or a guest you want to shelter from cold or rain. 잠깐 = 'briefly/for a moment' (slightly shorter feel than 잠시), 들어오세요 = 'please come in' (들어오다, 'enter toward the speaker'). The crucial grammar pair: 들어오다 ('come in', toward you as host) vs 들어가다 ('go in', away from the speaker) — as the host standing at your own door, you always say 들어오세요; 들어가세요 would mean 'go in (away from me)', which would be odd or imply you're pushing someone else into a space. Register: 존댓말 (들어오세요) for most guests; close friends get 들어와; the most polite form is the question 잠시 들어오시겠어요? which gives the visitor room to decline. Korean homes are shoes-off: saying this implicitly means the visitor should step up past the 현관 and remove shoes, so the follow-up 신발 벗으세요 may not even need to be said. The English-speaker trap is the direction error or replacing 들어오다 with bare 와요 ('come'), which loses the 'into the space' meaning.

structuredNuance.t: 잠깐 들어오세요 = 'briefly, please come in (toward me)'. 들어오다 = 'enter (in the direction of the speaker)'. The real meaning is a warm host invitation at the threshold — the speaker is already inside and welcoming someone toward their space.

존댓말 들어오세요 for most visitors. 반말 들어와 for close friends or younger people. Most polite: 잠시 들어오시겠어요? (a question, giving the visitor a graceful option to decline). Culturally, adding a reason (추운데, 비 오는데) or an offer (차 한잔 드시고 가세요) makes the invitation feel warm rather than perfunctory.

들어오세요 = 'come in (toward the speaker/host)'. 들어가세요 = 'go in (away from the speaker)' — a host never says 들어가세요 to a visitor at their own door. 앉으세요 ('please sit') follows once they're inside. Note: 오세요 alone ('please come') doesn't convey 'into the space'.
들어와 (반말) → 잠깐 들어오세요 → 잠시 들어오시겠어요? (가장 정중). Pairings: 추운데 들어오세요, 비 오는데 일단 들어오세요. Follow-ups: 신발 벗고 들어오세요, 앉으세요, 차 한잔 드실래요?

Saying 들어가세요 as a host — 들어가다 means 'go in (away from you)'; as the person already inside inviting someone toward you, it must be 들어오세요. Also: using bare 와요 ('come') without 들어- loses the 'into the space' meaning of the invitation.

mistakes: Saying 들어가세요 as a host — that's 'go in (away from me)'; inviting someone toward you is 들어오세요.
Using bare 와요 for 'come in' — 와요 is just 'come'; 'come inside' needs 들어오다 → 들어오세요.
Forgetting the shoes-off norm — after 들어오세요, expect to remove shoes at the 현관; barging in with shoes on is a real faux pas.

english: Please take your shoes off before coming in
usage: Please take your shoes off and come in.
존댓말 — host telling a guest the house rule
Take your shoes off and come in.
반말 — to a friend or younger visitor
You can take your shoes off and come in.
격식 — polite/neutral, e.g. a posted notice, reception desk, or formal host
Natural follow-up offering indoor slippers after shoes are removed
examples: A: 신발 벗고 들어오세요. / B: 아, 네!
A: Please take your shoes off. / B: Oh, sure!
The bare house rule and the guest's natural quick agreement; 아, 네 = a surprised but willing acknowledgment
여기 현관에서 신발 벗고 들어오시면 돼요.
You can take your shoes off here at the entrance and come in.
현관 names the exact spot (lowered entry area just inside the door) where shoes come off — the host is pointing to the right place
양말 안 신으셨으면 여기 덧신 있어요. 신발 벗고 들어오세요.
If you're not wearing socks, there are guest socks here. Please take your shoes off and come in.
Real hosting detail: offering 덧신 (disposable guest socks) with the shoes-off instruction shows attentiveness; many Korean hosts keep these by the 현관
nuance: Removing shoes at the 현관 (raised-threshold entrance area) is a firm and universal rule in Korean homes — not a suggestion, and not limited to traditional homes. A host may say this, but often just the visual of the shoes lined up at the 현관 and the raised floor level is enough of a cue. 신발 = shoes, 벗다 = take off (for footwear and clothing), -고 = 'and then', 들어오세요 = please come in. The verb pair is critical: 벗다 ('take off') vs 신다 ('put on' — specifically for footwear and legwear) — shoes/socks use 신다 to wear, 벗다 to remove, never 입다 (which is for upper/lower body clothing, not footwear). The physical boundary to internalize: the 현관 is a slightly sunken tiled area just inside the front door where outdoor footwear stays; the raised 마루 or 거실 floor is the shoes-free indoor space. Stepping over that threshold with shoes on is the most noticeable foreigner mistake in a Korean home. The English-speaker trap is mixing up 벗다 and 빼다 (빼다 = 'pull out/extract an object') — shoes are 벗다, not 빼다.

structuredNuance.t: 신발 벗고 들어오세요 = 'take off shoes AND THEN come in'. -고 sequences two actions. The real meaning is the universal Korean home rule: shoes stay in the 현관 (entry area), the indoor floor is shoes-free. This is non-negotiable in virtually every Korean home.

존댓말 벗고 들어오세요 (to guests, visitors, adults). 반말 벗고 들어와 (to friends, younger people). Formal/notice: 신발은 벗고 들어오시면 됩니다. As a guest, you can preempt: 신발 벗어도 될까요? ('may I take my shoes off?') — though it's always expected, asking shows cultural awareness.

벗다 = take off (shoes, socks, jacket, hat — any wearable item). 신다 = put on (specifically footwear and legwear: shoes, socks, stockings). 입다 = wear/put on (clothing on the torso or legs, NOT footwear). The follow-up 슬리퍼 신으세요 uses 신다 because slippers are footwear.
벗고 들어와 (반말) → 벗고 들어오세요 → 벗고 들어오시면 됩니다 (격식). Follow-ups: 슬리퍼 신으세요 (put on slippers), 덧신 있어요 (guest socks are here), 여기에 놓으세요 (put your shoes here).

Confusing 신다/벗다 with 입다/벗다 — 입다 is for clothing (shirt, pants), NOT footwear. Shoes and socks always use 신다 (put on) / 벗다 (take off). Also: 빼다 ('pull out') is wrong for removing shoes — it's 벗다. Walking onto the raised 거실/마루 floor with shoes is the most visible cultural mistake.

mistakes: Saying 신발을 입으세요 (wrong) instead of 신발을 신으세요 — footwear uses 신다 to put on, never 입다 (입다 is for clothing like shirts and pants, not for shoes or socks).
Stepping onto the 거실/마루 with shoes on — shoes come off at the 현관; the raised floor is shoes-free.
Translating 'take off' as 빼다 (신발 빼세요) — 빼다 is 'pull out/remove (an object)'; for shoes/clothes it's 벗다.

usage: 존댓말 — answering the door or intercom to an unknown caller
반말 — to family, or when you expect a friend
May I ask what brings you?
격식/정중 — softer; asks purpose rather than bluntly demanding identity
The typical answer you'll hear back through the door or intercom
examples: A: (딩동) 누구세요? / B: 택배입니다.
A: (Ding-dong) Who is it? / B: Delivery.
The standard intercom exchange when the bell rings; 택배입니다 = 'It's a parcel/courier' — no need for full sentences on the intercom
누구세요? 저희 집에 무슨 일이세요?
Who is it? What do you need from us?
Adding 무슨 일이세요? ('what is your business?') asks for their purpose politely; natural when you're cautious about an unexpected visitor
밤늦게 모르는 사람이 벨을 눌러서 문 안 열고 누구세요? 하고 물었어요.
A stranger rang late at night, so without opening I asked 'who is it?' through the door.
Real safety habit: 문 안 열고 ('without opening') + 누구세요? is the standard cautious protocol — you ask before you open, especially late at night
nuance: 누구세요? is the phrase you call through a closed door or the 인터폰 (intercom) when someone rings. 누구 = 'who', 세요 is the honorific present of 이다/되다 used for 'who are you?' — polite enough for any adult stranger. The two-way register split: 존댓말 누구세요? for unknowns and adults; 반말 누구야? for family or when you already know it's a close friend. The near-synonym 어떻게 오셨어요? ('what brings you?') softens the question by asking purpose rather than demanding identity, and is more appropriate once the door is slightly open or when you're fairly sure the person is legitimate. The critical English-speaker trap is answering a doorbell with 여보세요? — that phrase is strictly telephone hello; it sounds wrong at a physical door. Another trap: using 당신 누구예요? sounds confrontational and aggressive to a stranger (당신 as a second person is distancing and challenging in Korean); drop the subject entirely and say just 누구세요?. Korean home safety practice: always ask 누구세요? before opening the door, especially to unannounced visitors.

structuredNuance.t: 누구세요? = 'who are you?' (polite). The real use is specifically at a door, intercom, or through a closed barrier — asking identity before deciding whether to open. This is a safety function as much as a social one.

존댓말 누구세요? to any unknown adult at the door or intercom. 반말 누구야? to family members or when you're certain it's a friend. Most polite/indirect: 어떻게 오셨어요? ('what brings you?') — used when opening the door to someone who appears legitimate. Do not use 당신 누구예요? — the pronoun 당신 sounds challenging to a stranger.

누구세요? = direct identity question (who?), fine for an unknown buzz. 어떻게 오셨어요? = purpose question (what brings you?), softer and better face-to-face. 여보세요? = telephone hello ONLY — never use at a physical door. The choice signals how guarded or welcoming you are.
누구야? (반말) → 누구세요? → 어떻게 오셨어요? (가장 정중). Extensions: 누구세요? 무슨 일이세요? (who + what business?). If they don't answer: 잠깐만요 ('just a moment') while you check the CCTV.
Saying 여보세요? at the door — 여보세요 is the telephone greeting only; it sounds bizarre at a physical door. Also: 당신 누구예요? sounds confrontational; the subject-less 누구세요? is natural and polite.

mistakes: Answering the door with 여보세요? — that's the phone 'hello'; at a door or intercom say 누구세요?.
Adding 당신 (당신 누구예요?) — 당신 to a stranger sounds confrontational; the bare 누구세요? is correct.
Using 누구예요? flat — at the door the honorific 누구세요? is safer/politer to an unknown adult than plain 누구예요?.

usage: I just moved in next door.
존댓말 — greeting a neighbor as the new resident
반말 — to a friend or a peer-aged neighbor you're meeting informally
격식 — formal/humble phrasing; -게 되었습니다 = 'it came to be that I moved in', indirect and deferential
I hope we'll get along going forward.
The set closing phrase that almost always follows 이사 왔어요 — omitting it feels abrupt
examples: A: 안녕하세요, 옆집에 이사 왔어요. / B: 아, 반가워요!
A: Hi, I just moved in next door. / B: Oh, nice to meet you!
The bare newcomer greeting and a warm reply; 반가워요 = 'nice to meet you / glad to see you'
며칠 전에 이사 왔는데 인사가 늦었어요. 잘 부탁드려요.
I moved in a few days ago — sorry the greeting's a bit late. I hope we get along.
인사가 늦었어요 ('the greeting is late') is a polite self-deprecating touch that Koreans use to acknowledge the delay without over-apologizing
이사 왔는데 떡 좀 돌리려고요. 시끄럽게 했으면 죄송해요.
I just moved in and wanted to share some rice cakes. Sorry if we were noisy.
Real Korean custom: 떡 돌리다 ('distribute rice cakes') to neighbors when moving in — the offering softens any moving-day disturbance and builds 정 (warm connection)
nuance: Greeting neighbors as a new resident is a genuine social expectation in Korea, and 이사 왔어요 is the exact line you deliver at the neighbor's door. The directional verb is the key: 이사 오다 ('move in / come by moving') uses 오다 ('come') because you have arrived at your new location — you are now there. 이사 가다 (with 가다, 'go') means to move OUT or away from where you currently are, so saying 이사 갔어요 to a neighbor you've just met would mean you've left, the opposite meaning. Register: 존댓말 (왔어요) to any neighbor; 반말 to a peer-aged friend moving nearby; formal 이사 오게 되었습니다 to elderly neighbors or when you want to sound especially respectful. The phrase is almost always followed by 잘 부탁드립니다 ('please treat me well / let's get along') — this closing has no direct English equivalent but functions as a social contract-opener; leaving it out makes the greeting feel incomplete and slightly cold. The traditional custom of bringing 떡 (rice cakes) to neighbors on moving day is well-established but less universal in big city apartments now — even mentioning it shows cultural knowledge. The English-speaker trap is translating 'move' as 움직이다 ('move physically') or 이동하다 ('travel/shift location') — changing residence is 이사하다.

structuredNuance.t: 이사 왔어요 = 'I came by moving (here)'. 이사(移徙) = change of residence. 왔어요 = came (toward speaker's current location, 오다). The real meaning is 'I am the new neighbor' — this is the opening of a relationship, not just a statement of fact.

존댓말 이사 왔어요 to most neighbors. 이사 오게 되었습니다 (격식) to elderly neighbors or in a formal context — the -게 되었습니다 form sounds humble and deliberate. Always follow with 잘 부탁드립니다 (존댓말) or 잘 부탁해요 (informal). A small gift (떡, 과일) makes the greeting even warmer.

이사 왔어요 = moved IN to this place (오다, direction toward current location). 이사 갔어요 = moved OUT/away from a place (가다, direction away). The speaker always uses 왔어요 for their own arrival. 새로 이사 오신 분이에요? = 'Are you the new resident who moved in?' (asked by others about you).
이사 왔어 (반말) → 이사 왔어요 → 이사 오게 되었습니다 (격식). Fixed closing: 잘 부탁드립니다 / 앞으로 잘 부탁드려요. Optional: 며칠 전에 이사 왔어요 (added timing), 인사가 늦었어요 (late greeting apology).

Saying 이사 갔어요 to a new neighbor — 가다 = 'go away', meaning you left/moved out; arriving here is 이사 왔어요 (오다). Also: 움직였어요 ('I moved/budged physically') or 이동했어요 ('I traveled') are wrong for changing residence — that is 이사했어요 or 이사 왔어요.

mistakes: Saying 이사 갔어요 to a new neighbor — 가다 = 'go (away)', meaning you moved OUT; arriving here is 이사 왔어요 (오다).
Using 움직였어요 for 'I moved' — 움직이다 is physical motion/budging; changing residence is 이사하다.
Ending at 이사 왔어요 with nothing more — Koreans expect the follow-up 잘 부탁드립니다; omitting it sounds curt.
